title: Imaging and characterization of spontaneous vortices in a proximity-induced superconductor
authors: Iku Nakaaki, Kotaro Taki, Mio Nomura, Haruna Ishimaru, Minagi Yono, Jun Chen, Hiroyo Segawa, Akiko Nakamura, Taku Moronaga, Minoru Tachiki, Shuuichi Ooi, Shunichi Arisawa, Tsutomu Nojima, Takashi Uchino
abstract: Observation of spontaneous symmetry breaking is crucial to our understanding of a continuous second-order phase transition from a disordered system into an ordered one, which often leads to the formation of topological defects. In the case of superconductors, such topological defects are identified as quantized vortices. However, their geometrical characteristics have not been well investigated and understood yet. For the imaging of spontaneous vortices, we employ a proximity-coupled superconducting nanocomposite. Here we show from scanning superconducting quantum interference device microscope measurements that vortices with different polarities, size and shapes are observed stochastically especially under near zero-field conditions. The field distributions of the spontaneous vortices are more extended and intricate than those of the field induced Abrikosov vortices, yielding longer penetration depths ranging from ~1 to ~10 micrometer. The spontaneous vortices are created during cooling as a result of the competition between Josephson coupling and thermal phase fluctuation, both of which are inherently present in this proximity-coupled system. The morphology of the vortices most likely imprints the information that is frozen at the time of vortex formation, providing insights into the local phase differences that are present in the early stage of the phase transition.
summary: This work investigates spontaneous quantized vortices in a proximity-coupled superconducting nanocomposite using SSM imaging. By observing vortex characteristics under near-zero fields, the authors find that these defects are geometrically distinct from field-induced ones. This evidence strongly suggests that these vortices form via non-equilibrium processes related to phase coherence freezing during cooling.
main_problem: The study aims to understand the formation and characteristics of spontaneous quantized vortices, which are topological defects arising during a continuous second-order phase transition in superconductors.
main_result: Spontaneous vortices observed under near-zero fields exhibit significantly larger penetration depths ($\sim 1-10 \mu	ext{m}$) compared to field-induced ones, suggesting they exist in a non-equilibrium or quenched state rather than thermodynamic equilibrium.
method: The research employs scanning superconducting quantum interference device microscope (SSM) measurements on a proximity-coupled nanocomposite film to image local magnetic fields and current distributions.
model_or_system: The physical system is a proximity-coupled superconductor nanocomposite ($	ext{MgB}_2/	ext{MgO}$), modeled as an ensemble of Josephson junctions. The underlying physics relates to spontaneous symmetry breaking and defect formation dynamics, drawing parallels with the Kibble-Zurek mechanism.
key_observables: Vortex polarity, size, shape, local magnetic field distributions, estimated penetration depth ($\lambda$), and current density maps.
important_parameters: Near zero applied magnetic fields ($H \le \pm 0.25 	ext{ mOe}$), temperature near $T_c$, Josephson coupling energy ($E_J$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on fitting field profiles using the monopole model, which assumes certain geometric relationships that may be compromised for highly extended vortices.
figures_summary: Figures show schematic representations of phase coherence and defects (Fig. 1); structural/superconducting characterization ($	ext{XRD}$, $ho(T)$, $\chi'(T)$) (Fig. 2); SSM images demonstrating stochastic vortex generation in near-zero fields (Figs. 3, 4, 5a); and field profiles fitted to estimate large penetration depths (Figs. 3, 4, 5b/c).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the theoretical context of topological defects during phase transitions, detailing the experimental setup using nanocomposites, presenting measurements showing stochastic vortex formation in zero fields, and finally contrasting these spontaneous vortices with field-induced ones to conclude they are non-equilibrium structures.
why_interesting: The investigation into defect dynamics far from equilibrium provides a tangible platform for studying quench dynamics and phase transition universality, concepts central to statistical mechanics and many-body physics.

(b) At temperatures well below Tc, the entire system goes towards a global phase coherence state, in which the respective S domains have an identical phase state, owing to the proximity effect, although topological defects where the sum of the phases around a loop (represented by a red wavy circle) exceeds ±2𝜋 may be created during a thermal quench.
